name: Night/day return decomposition: the index premium accrues outside the regular session
source_claim: Cooper, Cliff and Gulen: 'the US equity premium over the last decade is solely due to overnight returns; returns during the night are strongly positive and returns during the day are close to zero and sometimes negative,' and this holds 'for individual stocks, equity indexes, and futures contracts on equity indexes.' For S&P 500 constituents 1993-2006 average night returns are 2.82-4.76 bps and day returns -2.85 to +0.22 bps. Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan (NY Fed SR917) independently report that essentially 100% of the US equity premium in E-mini futures is earned overnight, and give the inventory identity E[R_overnight] = (dollar order imbalance) x (return variance) / (risk-bearing capacity).

sources.title: Return Differences between Trading and Non-Trading Hours: Like Night and Day
sources.author_or_org: Michael J. Cooper, Michael T. Cliff, Huseyin Gulen
sources.what_it_measured: Close-to-open vs open-to-close returns for US stocks, indices and index futures, 1993-2006

sources.title: The Overnight Drift (Staff Report 917)
sources.author_or_org: Nina Boyarchenko, Lars Christian Larsen, Paul Whelan / Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.what_it_measured: 24-hour intraday decomposition of E-mini S&P 500 futures returns, 1998-2020, and the link to end-of-day order imbalance

sources.title: A tug of war: Overnight versus intraday expected returns
sources.author_or_org: Dong Lou, Christopher Polk, Spyros Skouras (Journal of Financial Economics)
sources.what_it_measured: Decomposition of momentum and reversal profits into overnight and intraday components; intraday 3-factor alpha +1.05% vs overnight -0.88% for the strategies studied

contradictory_evidence: Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan themselves published 'The Disappearing Overnight Drift' (Liberty Street Economics, July 2026) reporting that the 2:00-3:00 ET window that carried more than 60% of the E-mini's 5.9% annualized close-to-close return has 'generated close to zero' from January 2021 through December 2025, because the standard deviation of end-of-day relative signed volume fell from 6.5% to 2.9%. Lou/Polk/Skouras find the opposite sign for the cross-section (overnight reversal, intraday continuation), so night-positivity is not a universal law but a property of the aggregate index. Note also that this is beta timing, not market-neutral alpha: it inherits the full equity drawdown profile.
our_inference: We measured the 23-hour decomposition on our own store (ES and NQ, 2025-06-08 to 2026-09-10, roll-safe, bars excluded across contract changes and session breaks). ES accumulated +884.8 points in 18:00-08:59 ET, +242.2 points in 09:00-09:59, and +7.8 points in 10:00-15:59 over ~312 days. NQ accumulated +4018.0, -378.8 and +283.0 points in the same three windows. The overnight gap (16:00 ET close to 09:30 ET open) averaged +4.605 ES points (sd 35.26, n=312, t=2.31) and +24.04 NQ points (sd 208.4, t=2.04). OUR HYPOTHESIS, distinct from the sources: on this sample the entire ES advance is earned outside 10:00-15:59 ET, so a 'long overnight, flat during the regular session' schedule should beat buy-and-hold with roughly half the variance, at one round turn per session.
proposed_mechanism: Overnight is when risk cannot be hedged and inventory cannot be laid off. Liquidity providers who absorb the closing imbalance must carry the position through a period of thin depth, and they price that inventory risk into the close. The compensation is realised when depth returns as Europe and then the US open. It persists because the constraint is structural (the market is shut, and most institutional mandates cannot hold overnight-only exposure) rather than an arbitrage that capital can compete away without taking the same inventory risk.
observable_variables: close price at 16:00 ET (last regular-session minute bar)
open price at 09:30 ET next session
signed overnight return in points and in returns
trailing 20-session realised overnight volatility for scaling
per-hour cumulative return across the 23-hour cycle
session-complete flag (bar count and endpoint check per the existing loader convention)
failure_conditions: Killed if the mean overnight gap on a held-out half of the sample is not positive, or if the overnight Sharpe does not exceed the 10:00-15:59 Sharpe, or if the result is carried by fewer than 10 sessions (drop the top and bottom 2% of nights and re-measure; if the mean goes to zero it is a tail artefact, not a premium).
data_we_lack: End-of-day signed order imbalance, which is the actual state variable in the Boyarchenko identity. We can only proxy it with signed volume from 1-minute OHLCV (close location within the bar times volume), which is a weak substitute for the real closing-auction imbalance.
falsification_test: Split the ~312 sessions into the first and second half by date. Compute mean overnight gap and its t-statistic in each half separately for ES and NQ. If either half has a negative point estimate, or if the pooled t drops below 1.5 after winsorising nightly returns at the 2nd and 98th percentiles, the mechanism is dead for this sample.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points. Round-turn cost in ES points: ES $16.28 / $50 = 0.326 pts; MES $2.47 / $5 = 0.494 pts. Against a measured +4.605 pts per night, cost is 7.1% of gross in ES and 10.7% in MES. In NQ points: NQ $13.78 / $20 = 0.689 pts and MNQ $1.72 / $2 = 0.860 pts against +24.04 pts, i.e. 2.9% and 3.6%. This is the single most cost-tolerant mechanism in this file. Note the counter-intuitive ordering: the big contracts are cheaper PER POINT than the micros (0.326 vs 0.494 ES points), so if capital allows, ES beats MES on cost.
why_this_might_be_wrong: This is not alpha, it is a schedule for taking beta, and our sample is fifteen months of a market that rose. A +4.6 point mean with sd 35.3 and t=2.31 is one standard error away from +2.6, which is a much less interesting number, and the entire result could be the 2025-2026 bull tape rather than an inventory premium. The Fed authors who documented the mechanism have since published that its most identifiable component is gone. A backtest that holds overnight also carries the gap risk that the daytime-flat schedule is supposed to be avoiding, and our cost model does not include the overnight margin requirement.

name: The 02:00-03:00 ET inventory-unwind window (pre-registered by an external paper, tested out of sample here)
source_claim: Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan: 'almost 100 percent of the US equity premium is earned during a one-hour window between 2:00 a.m. and 3:00 a.m. ET,' coinciding with the European open, worth roughly 3.7% annualized and more than 60% of the E-mini's 5.9% annualized close-to-close return over 1998-2020. They attribute it to liquidity providers who absorbed the prior US close's order imbalance being relieved when European buyers arrive, and document an asymmetry: 'market selloffs generate robust positive overnight reversals, while reversals following market rallies are much more modest.'

sources.title: The Overnight Drift (Staff Report 917)
sources.author_or_org: Nina Boyarchenko, Lars Christian Larsen, Paul Whelan / Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.what_it_measured: Hour-by-hour returns on E-mini S&P 500 futures over the 24-hour cycle, 1998-2020, conditioned on prior-close order imbalance

sources.title: The Disappearing Overnight Drift
sources.author_or_org: Nina Boyarchenko, Lars Christian Larsen, Paul Whelan / Liberty Street Economics, Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.what_it_measured: The same 2:00-3:00 ET window extended to December 2025, plus the dispersion of end-of-day signed volume

contradictory_evidence: The strongest contradiction is from the original authors. Their July 2026 update states the 2:00-3:00 window 'generated close to zero' from January 2021 through December 2025, attributing the collapse to the standard deviation of end-of-day relative signed volume falling from 6.5% to 2.9% as algorithmic providers slice orders more finely. Volatility and overnight liquidity were unchanged; only the residual inventory transferred to counterparties shrank. They explicitly say the pattern would revive only if closing-imbalance dispersion widened again.
our_inference: We ran the pre-registered window on our store, roll-safe and gap-filtered. In ET hour 02:00-02:59 ES earned +0.821 points per day (t=1.93) and NQ +5.228 points per day (t=2.20). Across all 23 hours of the cycle this is the LARGEST positive hour for both instruments. Because the window was specified in advance by an external paper rather than selected by us, no multiple-testing correction applies to it, and t of 1.93 to 2.20 on a pre-registered window is real evidence. OUR HYPOTHESIS: the drift is not dead, it partially revived in 2025-2026, and our sample (2025-06 to 2026-09) barely overlaps the window the Fed authors declared dead (2021 to 2025-12). We also found ET hour 22:00-22:59 significantly NEGATIVE in both (ES -0.826, t=-2.13; NQ -4.815, t=-2.09), which is not in the source and which we treat as data-discovered and unproven.
proposed_mechanism: Inventory risk transfer with a delay. US closing imbalance is absorbed by dealers who cannot hedge it overnight; the position is unwound into the first deep external liquidity pool, which is the European cash open. The price concession paid at the US close is recovered at the European open, and the recovery is asymmetric because dealers absorbing a selloff are long an asset they do not want and pay more to get out than dealers who are short after a rally.
observable_variables: cumulative 1-minute return from 02:00:00 to 02:59:59 ET
signed close-window return 15:45-16:00 ET of the preceding session as the imbalance proxy
close-location-value weighted signed volume in the last 15 minutes of the prior regular session
trailing 20-day realised variance (the variance term in the Boyarchenko identity)
1-minute volume in 02:00-03:00 ET as a depth proxy
failure_conditions: Killed if the conditional version (long only when the prior close-window imbalance proxy was negative) does not beat the unconditional version, since the source's whole mechanism is imbalance-driven. Also killed if the effect is not present in both halves of the sample, or if the same-magnitude effect appears in three or more randomly chosen non-pre-registered hours (which would mean we are just measuring hourly noise at t=2).
data_we_lack: The actual end-of-day dollar order imbalance and the closing-auction print. The Fed's own diagnosis is that imbalance DISPERSION is the state variable that killed the effect; without the real imbalance series we cannot tell whether we are in a revived-dispersion regime or looking at noise.
falsification_test: For each of the 23 ET hours compute mean return per day and its t-statistic, on both halves of the sample, for ES and NQ. The 02:00 hour must rank in the top three positive hours in BOTH halves and BOTH instruments. If it ranks top in one half and mid-pack in the other, the fifteen-month result is noise and we stop.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in NQ points (NQ listed first because it is the cheaper leg here). Cost: NQ $13.78 / $20 = 0.689 NQ points, i.e. 13.2% of the measured +5.228. MNQ $1.72 / $2 = 0.860 points, 16.5%. In ES the arithmetic is much worse: 0.326 ES points against +0.821 is 39.7% of gross, and MES at 0.494 points is 60.2%, which fails the repo's own MAX_COST_SHARE=0.60 gate. Critical caveat we measured: ET hour 02:00 carries only 0.71% of ES daily volume versus 16.0% at 10:00, and the fraction of minutes quoted at one tick falls from 96.6% (15:00 ET) to 84.4% (02:00 ET), though the MEDIAN spread is 0.25 points at every hour of the 23-hour cycle. The $16.28 / $13.78 round-turn figures are regular-session-calibrated; assume 1.5x to 2x for a market order in this window, which pushes ES/MES firmly out and leaves NQ/MNQ marginal.
why_this_might_be_wrong: We are looking at the best of 23 hours and calling it pre-registered. That defence is real but it is not free: if the true effect is zero, the chance that a specific named hour shows t>1.9 is about 6%, and we ran it on two instruments that are 90% correlated, so it is close to one draw, not two. Fifteen months is 312 observations of a one-hour window. And we are directly contradicting the people who own the dataset and the mechanism, using a shorter sample, which is usually the wrong side of that bet.

name: Volatility-scaled noise-band breakout held to the close (intraday momentum, conditional form)
source_claim: Gao, Han, Li and Zhou (JFE 2018): the first half-hour return measured from the previous close predicts the last half-hour return, out-of-sample R-squared 1.7% with the first half-hour alone and 2.53% combined with the twelfth half-hour, stronger on high-volatility days, high-volume days, recession days and macro-release days. Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens (JFE 2021) extend it to more than 60 futures across equities, bonds, commodities and FX from 1974-2020 and find 'strong market intraday momentum everywhere,' with the last 30 minutes before the close positively predicted by the rest of the day, and the move 'reverts over the next days.' Zarattini, Barbon and Aziz (2024) trade the imbalance rather than the clock and report 1,985% cumulative, 19.6% annualized, Sharpe 1.33 net of costs, 2007 to early 2024 on SPY. An independent replication on futures reports, after $0.85 commission plus $1.40 exchange fees per contract per side and 0.25 tick slippage per side: ES 16.8% annual, Sharpe 1.25, +2 bps average per trade, 36% win rate, 2.09 payoff; NQ 24.3% annual, Sharpe 1.67, +6 bps average per trade, 38% win rate, 2.25 payoff, 2010 to present.

sources.author_or_org: Guido Baltussen, Zhi Da, Sten Lammers, Martin Martens (Journal of Financial Economics)

sources.title: Beat the Market: An Effective Intraday Momentum Strategy for S&P500 ETF (SPY)
sources.author_or_org: Carlo Zarattini, Andrea Barbon, Andrew Aziz / Concretum Research
sources.what_it_measured: Noise-area boundary from trailing same-time-of-day moves; breakout entries with trailing stops, exit at close; 2007 to early 2024

sources.title: Intraday Momentum for ES and NQ
sources.author_or_org: Quantitativo
sources.what_it_measured: Independent replication of the noise-area strategy on ES and NQ minute data from Databento, 2010-present, with explicit commission, exchange fee and slippage assumptions

contradictory_evidence: Mesfin (arXiv 2605.04004, May 2026, revised July 2026) ran fourteen momentum signal families on 947 days of 5-minute MNQ data (2021-2025) requiring out-of-sample validation, t>2.0, at least 30 trades, positive net return after a two-point round-trip friction, and yearly consistency. None of the fourteen families passed. Gross returns were approximately 0.07 to 1.50 points per trade, 'well below the assumed two-point friction cost.' Two positive controls did survive: an RTH Confluence Signal (t=5.83, +15.77 points mean, 538 trades) and a London Session Signal B (t=5.15, +5.77 points mean, 289 trades) - note that BOTH survivors are session/time-of-day constructs, not plain momentum. Separately, Ho et al. (2021) found no intraday momentum in the Australian market; the published academic version's costs receive far less rigorous treatment than its statistics; and the effect's strongest years in every published sample are 2008 and 2020.
our_inference: The published magnitude is expressed per trade in basis points, which is the form that matters for our binding constraint. ES +2 bps of a ~$380,000 notional is +1.52 ES points net per trade; NQ +6 bps of a ~$588,000 notional is +17.6 NQ points net per trade. Those were computed at a round turn of roughly $10.75 for ES (their $4.50 in fees plus 0.5 tick of slippage), whereas our measured ES round turn is $16.28, a difference of only 0.11 ES points. So the published net edge survives our cost basis arithmetically. OUR HYPOTHESIS: what distinguishes this from the plain breakout family the lab already killed is three things at once - the entry threshold is a volatility-scaled band built from trailing same-time-of-day moves rather than a fixed level, the exit is the close rather than a fixed bar count, and the win rate is deliberately low (36-38%) with a payoff ratio above 2. We should expect roughly half the published edge after post-publication decay, so we budget ~8 NQ points net per trade rather than 17.6.
proposed_mechanism: Baltussen et al.'s explanation is gamma hedging. Option market makers who are net short gamma, and leveraged and inverse ETFs that must rebalance to a constant multiple of a moving index, are all forced to trade in the direction the market has already moved, and the size of the required trade is convex in the move. Cheng and Madhavan's model puts leveraged ETF flow at 16.8% of market-on-close volume after a 1% index move and 50% after a 5% move, with rebalancing beginning about 20 minutes before the close; industry reporting in 2026 put daily leveraged ETF rebalancing at a record $50bn and 1.60% of total S&P 500 futures volume. The flow is price-insensitive and its timing is known, which is why it survives being public: to arbitrage it you must take the other side of a forced trade into the close and carry it.
observable_variables: trailing 14-day mean absolute move from the session open to each minute of the day, per minute-of-day, giving an upper and lower noise boundary anchored at the open
current price versus that boundary
session VWAP from 1-minute OHLCV (typical price times volume, cumulative)
signed rest-of-day return (09:30 to 15:15)
realised volatility of the session so far as the gamma-magnitude proxy
minutes remaining to 16:00 ET
failure_conditions: Killed if net points per trade is below the cost line in either half of the sample; if the result depends on more than 10 sessions (drop the best 10 trades and re-measure); if the win rate is above 50% (that would mean we are not trading the mechanism described but something else); or if a fixed-level breakout with the same turnover performs as well, which would mean the volatility scaling contributes nothing and we have merely rebuilt the family the lab already rejected.
data_we_lack: Dealer gamma exposure (GEX) and leveraged/inverse ETF assets under management, which are the actual conditioning variables in the source. We can only proxy the hedging pressure with the size of the day's move and realised volatility, both of which are available. Options data would let us condition properly, and the repo's Theta Data options plan has lapsed to FREE per the O-3 commit.
falsification_test: Build the noise band exactly as specified (14-day trailing same-minute-of-day absolute moves anchored at the session open), take breakouts, exit at 15:45 ET or on a return inside the band, and charge $16.28 per ES round turn / $13.78 per NQ. If the mean net points per trade is not positive with t>2.0 on the second half of the sample, held out and never inspected while building the band, it is dead.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in NQ points. Cost per round turn: NQ 0.689 points, MNQ 0.860 points. Against our discounted expectation of 8.0 net points the cost share is 7.9% (NQ) and 9.7% (MNQ); against the replication's unadjusted 17.6 points it is 3.8%. At 1.4 trades per session the daily cost is 0.96 NQ points, well inside the 1-3 round turns per session band that the prior 240-trial study found profitable 33% of the time. In ES: cost 0.326 points against a discounted ~0.8 net ES points (half of 1.52), a 29% cost share, still passing but with far less margin - NQ is the instrument for this mechanism.
why_this_might_be_wrong: This is a trend-continuation strategy and the lab's prior study found trend and volume-continuation losing at t as low as -13 on train and -6 on validation. My defence is that the conditioning and the hold-to-close exit make it a different animal, but I cannot prove that from outside, and the honest reading is that I am arguing an exception on the strength of a practitioner backtest whose two headline numbers (36% win rate, 2.09 payoff) mean the whole result lives in the right tail, where fifteen months of data has almost no resolution. The Mesfin falsification study is on our exact instrument, our exact bar type and an overlapping period, and it says no.

name: Last-45-minute continuation conditional on the size of the rest-of-day move (gamma-convexity form)
source_claim: Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens: returns during the last 30 minutes before the close are positively predicted by returns during the rest of the day, across more than 60 futures markets from 1974 to 2020, and the predictive power is 'economically and statistically highly significant.' The mechanism is that hedging short gamma requires trading in the direction of price movements. Gao et al. add that the effect is stronger on high-volatility days, high-volume days and macro-release days. Cheng and Madhavan put leveraged ETF rebalancing at 16.8% of market-on-close volume after a 1% move and 50% after a 5% move, with orders starting around 20 minutes before the close.

sources.title: Hedging demand and market intraday momentum
sources.author_or_org: Guido Baltussen, Zhi Da, Sten Lammers, Martin Martens (Journal of Financial Economics)
sources.what_it_measured: Rest-of-day return predicting last-30-minute return in 60+ futures, and the contribution of option market maker and leveraged ETF gamma hedging

sources.title: Market Intraday Momentum
sources.author_or_org: Lei Gao, Yufeng Han, Sophia Zhengzi Li, Guofu Zhou (Journal of Financial Economics)
sources.what_it_measured: Conditioning of the last-half-hour predictability on volatility, volume, recessions and macro releases

sources.title: Leveraged ETFs, Option Market Imbalances, and End-of-Day Price Dynamics
sources.author_or_org: Heiner Beckmeyer et al. (Northern Finance Association / University of St. Gallen)
sources.what_it_measured: Joint effect of leveraged ETF rebalancing and option market maker imbalances on end-of-day price dynamics

sources.title: Leveraged ETF Rebalancing Hits $50 Billion
sources.author_or_org: Benzinga
sources.what_it_measured: Current scale of daily leveraged ETF rebalancing flow: fourfold increase since start of 2026, 1.60% of total S&P 500 futures volume

contradictory_evidence: Mesfin's MNQ falsification study (arXiv 2605.04004) found no momentum family clearing a two-point friction on 2021-2025 MNQ data, which covers most of the period in which the leveraged ETF flow was supposedly growing. The Gao et al. version is an ETF result from a sample ending in 2013 and secondary summaries of it explicitly warn that the research period ended in 2013 and that effects like this can shrink once published. Note also that the mechanism cuts both ways: dealers who are net LONG gamma trade against the move, damping it. Without the actual gamma exposure sign we may be assuming the wrong side of the market on any given day.
our_inference: Measured on our store over ~313 complete sessions: the mean absolute move in 15:15-15:45 ET is 6.64 ES points and 32.00 NQ points, and in 15:45-16:00 ET it is 6.78 ES points and 31.96 NQ points. So the final 45 minutes of the regular session carries a mean absolute move of roughly 10-13 ES points, and ET hour 15:00-15:59 alone carries 15.7% of ES daily volume, second only to 10:00. There is plenty of movement to capture. OUR HYPOTHESIS: the predictability is not in the sign of the rest-of-day return alone (the lab already killed plain continuation) but in the interaction of sign with magnitude, because the hedging requirement is convex in the move - condition the trade on |rest-of-day return| being in the top tercile of its trailing distribution and take the sign, otherwise stand aside. That reduces turnover to roughly one trade every three sessions and concentrates it where the flow is largest.
proposed_mechanism: Constant-leverage products and short-gamma dealers face a rebalancing requirement proportional to the square of the day's move (leveraged ETF flow scales as the move times AUM times a leverage factor; short-gamma delta drift scales as gamma times the move). That flow must execute near the close and is price-insensitive. On small-move days the flow is negligible and the last 45 minutes is noise. On large-move days the flow is a material fraction of closing volume and pushes price further in the same direction. The effect persists because the flow is mandatory, its timing is public, and taking the other side means carrying the position through the close.
observable_variables: signed return from the 09:30 ET open to 15:15 ET
absolute value of that return divided by its trailing 60-session mean, giving the conditioning tercile
realised volatility of the 09:30-15:15 window from 1-minute bars
cumulative volume in 15:00-15:45 versus its trailing average
return in 15:15-16:00 ET (the predicted window)
sign agreement between the overnight gap and the rest-of-day move
failure_conditions: Killed if the top-tercile-magnitude subset does not outperform the unconditional version, since the convexity is the entire claim. Also killed if the effect is present only when the predicted window is extended past 16:00 ET, which would mean we are trading the post-settlement drift (MR-05) rather than the close. Also killed if the sign of the effect flips between ES and NQ.
data_we_lack: Dealer net gamma exposure and its sign, and leveraged ETF AUM. This is the biggest gap in the file: the source's mechanism predicts CONTINUATION when dealers are net short gamma and DAMPING when they are net long, and we cannot observe which regime we are in. Options open interest by strike (a lapsed Theta Data subscription) would resolve it.
falsification_test: Regress the 15:15-16:00 ET return on the signed 09:30-15:15 return interacted with the magnitude tercile, on ES and NQ separately, on the first half of the sample only. If the top-tercile interaction coefficient is not positive with t>2 in both instruments, stop. If it passes, trade it on the held-out half at $16.28 / $13.78 per round turn and require positive net points per trade.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) against an expected 1.0 net point, i.e. a 33% cost share in ES and 49% in MES - MES is inside but close to the repo's 0.60 MAX_COST_SHARE gate. In NQ the same 15% capture of a 32.0-point mean absolute move is ~4.8 NQ points against 0.689 (NQ) or 0.860 (MNQ), cost shares of 14% and 18%, which is comfortable. At 0.35 trades per session this sits at the very low end of the turnover band the prior study found survivable. The capture assumption (15% of the mean absolute window move) is the load-bearing guess here and should be the first thing measured.
why_this_might_be_wrong: The single largest problem is that our regular-session convention ends at 15:45 ET while the effect the sources document peaks in 15:30-16:00 and settles at 16:00. If the lab tests this on the 09:30-15:45 window it will be testing two thirds of the window with the most important third missing, and a null result would be uninformative. Beyond that: 15% capture of the mean absolute move is a number I invented for the feasibility arithmetic, not one any source supports, and if the true capture is 4% the mechanism fails in ES and is marginal in NQ.

name: Closing-period price pressure reverses in the 16:00-17:00 ET post-settlement window
source_claim: NYSE research and the closing-auction literature: large institutional flows in the last minutes, particularly the closing auction, cause temporary price pressure followed by reversal, and roughly 83% of the closing price impact reverses over the next three to five days. Closing price deviations 'reverse almost fully overnight, with one-third to one-half of the reversal occurring within the first half-hour after the close for stocks with sufficient after-hours liquidity,' which suggests auction volume is to a significant extent uninformed. Boyarchenko et al. supply the pricing identity: the overnight return is the dollar order imbalance times return variance divided by risk-bearing capacity, so the closing imbalance IS the predictor.

sources.title: The last minutes of the trading day have a big impact
sources.author_or_org: Alpha Architect
sources.what_it_measured: Summary of end-of-day price pressure and reversal evidence

contradictory_evidence: The reversal evidence is overwhelmingly about SINGLE STOCKS with idiosyncratic auction imbalances, where an index future has no auction at all and its closing imbalance is diversified across 500 names, so the index-level imbalance should be far smaller relative to depth. Baltussen et al. cut the other way for the index: they find the close-period move is momentum, not pressure, and only reverts 'over the next days,' not within the hour. And the Fed's own 2026 update says end-of-day imbalance dispersion has halved, which shrinks exactly the quantity this mechanism trades. Finally, ET hour 16:00-16:59 carries only 4.0% of ES daily volume in our store, so any measured reversal there could be a quoting artefact rather than a tradeable move.
our_inference: This mechanism is only testable because our data is far larger than the brief describes: the store runs the full 23-hour CME cycle (18:00 ET through 16:59 ET), not the 09:30-15:45 regular session. We measured mean absolute moves of 6.78 ES / 31.96 NQ points in 15:45-16:00 ET and 6.14 ES / 32.97 NQ points in 16:00-16:59 ET, with a median quoted spread of 0.25 ES points in BOTH hours and 92.7% of minutes at one tick in hour 16. So there is a real, quotable, similarly sized move in the hour after settlement. OUR HYPOTHESIS: the signed 15:45-16:00 move is a mixture of information and forced-flow pressure, the pressure component is mean-reverting, and a fade of that move entered at 16:00 ET and held to 16:59 ET should capture the pressure component while the information component washes out.
proposed_mechanism: Index-tracking funds, ETF creation/redemption arbitrage and market-on-close orders must print at or near the settlement price. The dealers who fill them take the opposite inventory and are unhedged the moment the auction clears. In the hour after settlement the same dealers work out of that inventory into whatever liquidity remains, and price retraces the concession. It persists because participation in the close is mandatory for the flow (benchmark tracking) and because taking the other side requires holding index risk through the thinnest hour of the US day.
observable_variables: signed return 15:45 ET to 16:00 ET
that return divided by the session's realised volatility
close-location value of each of the last 15 minute bars times its volume, summed, as a signed pressure proxy
volume in 15:45-16:00 relative to its trailing 20-session mean
return 16:00 ET to 16:59 ET (the predicted window)
quoted spread from ES_quotes.parquet in 16:00-17:00 as the realisable-cost check
failure_conditions: Killed if the fade is not stronger when the 15:45-16:00 volume spike is larger, since flow pressure is the whole story. Killed if the effect exists only on days when the 15:45-16:00 move was in the same direction as the rest of the day (that would be MR-04's continuation unwinding, a different mechanism). Killed if the realised spread cost in 16:00-17:00, measured from ES_quotes.parquet rather than assumed, exceeds 0.5 ES points per round turn.
data_we_lack: The actual closing-auction imbalance (published by the primary listing exchanges at 15:50 ET) and the futures settlement print itself. The auction imbalance is the true state variable; our close-location-weighted signed volume is a crude proxy that cannot distinguish an aggressive seller from a passive one.
falsification_test: Regress the 16:00-16:59 ET return on the signed, volatility-normalised 15:45-16:00 return, on ES and NQ separately. The coefficient must be negative with t>2 in both instruments and in both halves of the sample. Then charge the ACTUAL measured spread in that hour (from ES_quotes.parquet, not the regular-session $16.28) and require positive net points per trade.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points, assuming a 13% capture of the 6.78-point mean absolute close-window move. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) against 0.9 points is 36% and 55%; MES is at the edge of the 0.60 gate and ES is comfortable. In NQ, a 13% capture of 31.96 points is 4.2 points against 0.689 (NQ) or 0.860 (MNQ), i.e. 16% and 20%. The important caveat is that the $16.28 / $13.78 figures are calibrated on regular-session execution and hour 16 carries only 4.0% of daily volume, so a realised-cost check against ES_quotes.parquet must be part of the test rather than an afterthought. The median spread in that hour is still 0.25 points, which is encouraging.
why_this_might_be_wrong: The entire reversal literature I am leaning on is about single stocks with auction imbalances, and an index future does not have an auction. Diversification across 500 names should cancel most idiosyncratic pressure, leaving only the systematic component, which is exactly the component that is informative rather than mechanical. It is quite possible that the index-level close move is nearly all information, in which case there is nothing to fade and the 13% capture assumption is worth zero.

name: Asymmetric reversal of the overnight gap during the regular session
source_claim: Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan document 'an asymmetric reaction to demand shocks: market selloffs generate robust positive overnight reversals, while reversals following market rallies are much more modest.' Grant, Wolf and Yu (Journal of Banking and Finance, 2005) find intraday price reversals in the US stock index futures market over a 15-year sample, specifically reversals after overnight periods that carry very bad news, with the rebound occurring with a short delay during the first part of the trading day. Liu, Liu, Wang, Zhou and Zhu show that sorting on past OVERNIGHT returns and harvesting the subsequent INTRADAY return yields Sharpe ratios two to five times larger than conventional close-to-close reversal, and that the result holds for equity index, interest rate, commodity and currency futures. Cooper, Cliff and Gulen note the night-day effect 'is driven in part by high opening prices which subsequently decline in the first hour of trading.'

sources.title: The Overnight Drift (Staff Report 917)
sources.author_or_org: Nina Boyarchenko, Lars Christian Larsen, Paul Whelan / Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.what_it_measured: Asymmetry of overnight reversals conditional on the sign of the preceding demand shock in E-mini futures

sources.title: Intraday price reversals in the US stock index futures market: A 15-year study
sources.author_or_org: Terry Grant, Avner Wolf, Susana Yu (Journal of Banking and Finance)
sources.what_it_measured: Reversals in US stock index futures following large overnight moves, over a 15-year sample

sources.title: Overnight-Intraday Reversal Everywhere
sources.author_or_org: Chun Liu, Yang Liu, Tianyu Wang, Guofu Zhou, Yingzi Zhu
sources.what_it_measured: Long low-past-overnight-return, short high-past-overnight-return, harvesting intraday returns, across international stocks and equity index, rate, commodity and FX futures

sources.title: Return Differences between Trading and Non-Trading Hours: Like Night and Day
sources.author_or_org: Michael J. Cooper, Michael T. Cliff, Huseyin Gulen
sources.what_it_measured: Overnight versus daytime returns and the first-hour decline following high opens

contradictory_evidence: The Liu/Liu/Wang/Zhou/Zhu result is CROSS-SECTIONAL - it is a long/short portfolio across many assets, and we have only two economically distinct instruments (ES and NQ; MES and MNQ are the same underlyings). A two-asset cross-section is not a cross-section. Separately, Mesfin's MNQ study reports directly that 'gap fill fade strategies fail at every tested entry time,' that MNQ gaps do not consistently fill within the regular session, and that 'the market is as likely to continue in the gap direction as to reverse.' Our own store also contradicts the Cooper/Cliff/Gulen first-hour-decline sub-claim for ES: ET hours 9 and 10 are both positive (+0.776 and +0.564 points per day), though for NQ they are both negative (-1.21 and -1.85), so the sub-claim holds for one instrument and not the other.
our_inference: Mean absolute overnight gap (16:00 ET close to 09:30 ET open) is 25.92 ES points and 151.07 NQ points over 312 nights, which is comparable in size to the entire regular session's mean absolute move (32.66 ES, 176.10 NQ). The gap is the largest single price event in the daily cycle and it is where the whole drift lives. OUR HYPOTHESIS, and the part that distinguishes it from the plain reversion the lab already killed: the conditioning variable is the OVERNIGHT return, not any intraday return, and the expected relationship is ASYMMETRIC and one-sided - large negative gaps should be bought during the regular session and large positive gaps should NOT be sold. Trading only the down-gap tail cuts turnover to roughly one session in five and puts the trade where both the Fed's asymmetry finding and Grant/Wolf/Yu's bad-news reversal finding point.
proposed_mechanism: A large negative overnight gap is, in the inventory framework, evidence of a demand shock that liquidity providers absorbed at a concession while depth was thin. When the US regular session opens, the deepest pool of the day arrives, the concession is no longer necessary, and price retraces. The asymmetry exists because the risk-bearing capacity constraint binds harder on the downside: dealers forced long into falling prices face margin and VaR limits, while dealers short into a rally do not face the same convex constraint. It persists because being the buyer of a gap-down requires taking exactly the risk everyone else is shedding.
observable_variables: overnight gap = 09:30 ET open minus prior 16:00 ET close
gap divided by trailing 20-session standard deviation of the overnight gap
sign of the gap (the asymmetry switch)
the 18:00-09:29 ET path from 1-minute bars, so we can separate a gap that happened at 03:00 from one that happened at 09:00
return from 09:30 ET to 15:45 ET (the harvested window)
ES gap minus NQ gap in volatility units, as the two-asset relative-value version
failure_conditions: Killed if the effect is symmetric, since the asymmetry is the whole reason this is not the plain gap-fade that has already been falsified on MNQ. Killed if it does not strengthen as the gap gets larger in volatility units. Killed if the mean is positive only because of one or two crash days - drop the three largest down-gaps and re-measure.
data_we_lack: The cross-section. The published futures result is a portfolio sorted across dozens of contracts; we have two. We also lack the dollar order imbalance that identifies the demand shock, and any news feed that would let us separate an informed gap (bad earnings, a rate decision) from a flow gap, which is precisely the distinction the mechanism turns on.
falsification_test: Sort the 312 sessions into quintiles by volatility-normalised overnight gap. Compute the mean 09:30-15:45 ET return in each quintile for ES and NQ. The mechanism requires the bottom quintile (largest down-gaps) to be significantly positive with t>2 while the top quintile is NOT significantly negative. If both tails reverse symmetrically, or if neither does, it is dead.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points, assuming a ~6% capture of the 25.92-point mean absolute gap on the conditioned subset. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) against 1.5 points is 22% and 33%. In NQ a 6% capture of 151.07 points is 9.1 points against 0.689 (NQ) or 0.860 (MNQ), i.e. 7.6% and 9.5%. At 0.4 trades per session this is the second-lowest turnover mechanism in the file that still has enough observations to measure: roughly 62 trades in the down-gap quintile over fifteen months, which is above the repo's MIN_TRADES=40 floor but not by much.
why_this_might_be_wrong: Sixty-two trades is a thin basis for a claim about a conditional tail, and the tail is exactly where fifteen months of a calm bull market has the fewest observations. The published result I am leaning hardest on is cross-sectional and I am converting it to a time-series bet on two correlated assets, which is not the same statistical object. And the one study that ran the closest thing to this test on our exact instrument concluded gap fades fail at every entry time.

name: Multi-day reversal of the hedging-driven close move
source_claim: Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens state that the market intraday momentum they document - the last-30-minute move predicted by the rest of the day - 'reverts over the next days.' This is the direct implication of their mechanism: gamma hedging and leveraged-ETF rebalancing are forced, price-insensitive flows that move price away from fundamentals, so the displacement must be temporary. The closing-auction literature gives the same shape with a number attached for stocks: roughly 83% of the closing price impact reverses over the next three to five days.

sources.title: Hedging demand and market intraday momentum
sources.author_or_org: Guido Baltussen, Zhi Da, Sten Lammers, Martin Martens (Journal of Financial Economics)
sources.what_it_measured: Last-30-minute continuation across 60+ futures and its reversion over subsequent days

sources.title: Closing Auction: Immediate market impact, price drift and transaction cost of trading
sources.author_or_org: NYSE Data Insights
sources.what_it_measured: The 83% reversal of closing price impact over three to five days

sources.title: Market Closure and Short-Term Reversal
sources.author_or_org: Pasquale Della Corte, Robert Kosowski
sources.what_it_measured: Short-term reversal as compensation for liquidity provision, and the role of market closure and VIX in predicting it

contradictory_evidence: Baltussen et al. assert the reversion qualitatively and give no magnitude for it, which means the claim I am building on is the weakest-supported statement in this file. The 83% figure is from single stocks, where auction imbalances are idiosyncratic and large relative to depth. Della Corte and Kosowski's framing implies the reversal is compensation for liquidity provision, which means the return is earned by taking real risk (it is 'naturally short volatility' and pays best after large declines), not by exploiting a mispricing - so it should show a bad left tail exactly when the lab most needs capital preservation. And the lab has already killed plain reversion at the intraday horizon; the only thing new here is the horizon.
our_inference: Nothing in the prior 240-trial study tested a multi-day holding period, and the study's own finding - profitability falling monotonically with turnover, 1-3 round turns per session profitable 33% of the time versus over 10 per session profitable 4% - points directly at horizons LONGER than a session as the unexplored direction with the best cost arithmetic. OUR HYPOTHESIS: take the signed 15:15-16:00 ET move, normalise by session realised volatility, and fade the extreme decile over the following one to three sessions. At 0.33 round turns per session this is an order of magnitude below anything the study tested, and the position is held across two overnight periods, which is where MR-01 says the drift lives - so the long leg gets the overnight premium for free and the short leg pays it.
proposed_mechanism: Forced end-of-day flow displaces price. The displacement is not corrected instantly because the correction requires someone to warehouse index risk over multiple days, which is capital-expensive and mark-to-market risky. The correction therefore leaks out over the following sessions as slower capital arrives. It persists because the arbitrage is a multi-day inventory commitment rather than a round trip, which is the exact kind of trade that leverage constraints and daily risk limits prevent.
observable_variables: signed return 15:15 ET to 16:00 ET, normalised by the session's realised volatility
its decile rank within a trailing 120-session window
cumulative return over the following 1, 2 and 3 sessions measured close-to-close at 16:00 ET
session realised volatility and the trailing volatility ratio, as the regime filter
the overnight component of the holding period, tracked separately so the MR-01 premium can be netted out
failure_conditions: Killed if the reversal, measured on the extreme decile, is not larger than the unconditional multi-day mean return with the long/short sign built in - i.e. if it is just the MR-01 overnight premium wearing a reversal costume. That test must be run first. Also killed if the effect requires more than 3 sessions of holding, which would put it in the daily track's territory rather than this one.
data_we_lack: Nothing material for the test itself. What we lack is the ability to distinguish a flow-driven close move from an information-driven one, which is the whole basis for expecting reversion; options gamma exposure or a news feed would provide it. We also only have ~15 months, so the extreme-decile subset is roughly 31 events.
falsification_test: For the top and bottom decile of volatility-normalised 15:15-16:00 ET moves, compute the mean 1-, 2- and 3-session forward return. The reversal must be significant with t>2 AFTER subtracting the unconditional forward return over the same horizon (which removes the overnight drift and the market's trend). If the excess is not significant, it is dead.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) against an expected 2.0 points is 16% and 25%. Per SESSION the cost burden is 0.33 x 0.326 = 0.11 ES points, which is the lowest of any actively traded mechanism in this file. This is the profile the prior study's turnover finding argues for. The offsetting cost the arithmetic does NOT capture is overnight margin and gap risk over two nights, which is a capital cost rather than a transaction cost and does not appear in the $16.28 figure.
why_this_might_be_wrong: The source states the reversion in one clause and never quantifies it, so my 2.0-point expectation is an extrapolation from a stock-market number (83% over 3-5 days) to an index future where the pressure should be far smaller relative to depth. With roughly 31 events per decile over fifteen months, this test has almost no power: a true effect of 2 points against a 3-day return standard deviation of maybe 50 ES points would need hundreds of events to detect. The honest expectation is that this comes back inconclusive rather than either confirmed or killed.

name: Same-time-of-day return continuation at exact multiples of one trading day
source_claim: Heston, Korajczyk and Sadka (Journal of Finance, 2010) find 'a striking pattern of return continuation at half-hour intervals that are exact multiples of a trading day,' persisting for at least 40 trading days, more pronounced for but not restricted to the first and last half-hour periods. Volume, order imbalance, volatility and bid-ask spreads show similar periodicity but do not explain the return pattern, and the effect is not driven by firm size, systematic risk, S&P 500 membership, month of year, day of week or turn-of-month. The authors attribute it to institutional order splitting - large orders worked over many days at the same time of day.

sources.title: Intraday Patterns in the Cross-section of Stock Returns
sources.author_or_org: Steven L. Heston, Robert A. Korajczyk, Ronnie Sadka (Journal of Finance 65:4)
sources.what_it_measured: Half-hourly cross-sectional return autocorrelation at lags that are exact multiples of one trading day, US stocks

sources.title: Infrequent Rebalancing, Return Autocorrelation, and Seasonality
sources.author_or_org: Vincent Bogousslavsky (Journal of Finance 71:6)
sources.what_it_measured: A model in which infrequent rebalancing generates return autocorrelation that switches sign and becomes positive exactly at the rebalancing horizon

contradictory_evidence: The result is cross-sectional. It is about which STOCK outperforms at 10:30 today given which stock outperformed at 10:30 yesterday, and the source explicitly says it survives controls for S&P 500 membership - meaning it is idiosyncratic, not index-level. Order splitting by definition happens in single names; an index future has no single institution working a multi-day order in it at a fixed time of day in a way that would show up above the noise. Bogousslavsky's model likewise predicts the autocorrelation at the REBALANCING horizon, and index futures are the instrument institutions use precisely to AVOID committing to a rebalancing schedule.
our_inference: OUR HYPOTHESIS is the weakest in this file and we flag it as such: the time-series analogue on a single index future is the autocorrelation of the return in minute-of-day bin k with the return in bin k on the previous 1 to 40 sessions - a lag-375-minute autocorrelation rather than a cross-sectional sort. Even if the cross-sectional effect is real, the index-level version should be an order of magnitude smaller because it survives only the component of order splitting that is common across names. WE ARE INCLUDING THIS MECHANISM PRIMARILY AS A FLAGGED FAILURE: the brief asked us to flag any mechanism whose implied edge cannot clear its own costs, and this is that mechanism. It is listed so the lab does not spend a cycle rediscovering the arithmetic.
proposed_mechanism: Large institutional orders are split across days and executed at similar times of day, either because of a VWAP schedule anchored to the clock or because of a desk's habitual working hours. The residual demand at a given time of day therefore repeats, producing positive autocorrelation at exactly one-day lags. It would persist because the splitting is driven by market-impact minimisation, which is a real cost the institution is paying to avoid, not an error it will correct.
observable_variables: return in each 30-minute bin of the regular session (13 bins from 09:30 to 16:00)
the same bin's return on each of the previous 40 sessions
the lag-k autocorrelation of same-bin returns, k = 1 to 40 sessions
a control set of autocorrelations at NON-multiples of one day, which must be near zero for the claim to be about periodicity rather than general persistence
failure_conditions: Pre-declared as likely dead. It is killed unless the same-bin lag-1-day autocorrelation is positive with t>3 (not 2 - we are testing 13 bins times 40 lags and must pay for it) AND the corresponding non-multiple-of-a-day lags are indistinguishable from zero. Anything less and the arithmetic below applies.
data_we_lack: The cross-section of individual equities, which is where the documented effect actually lives. With SPY-constituent minute data or even 30 large-cap minute series this becomes the test the source ran; with four index futures it does not.
falsification_test: Compute the 13x40 matrix of same-bin lagged autocorrelations for ES and NQ, plus a matched control matrix at lags offset by half a session. If the multiple-of-a-day cells are not distinguishable from the control cells at t>3, the mechanism is dead for index futures. This is a one-hour test and should be run before any capital-allocating work, purely to close the question.
cost_feasibility_note: THIS MECHANISM FAILS ITS OWN COST TEST AND IS FLAGGED AS SUCH. Magnitude is in ES points. The HKS cross-sectional effect is a few basis points per 30-minute bin; the index-level residual should be well under 1 bp. One basis point of ES at 7,600 is 0.76 points, and a realistic index-level residual of 0.2-0.3 bps is 0.15-0.23 ES points. Against a round-turn cost of 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES), the cost EXCEEDS the entire expected gross edge - a cost share above 100%, versus the repo's 0.60 gate. To clear cost in ES the effect would have to be at least 0.43 bps per bin, roughly double the most generous index-level estimate, and it would have to hold at one round turn per session. Do not build this.
why_this_might_be_wrong: The strongest objection to including it at all is that I am converting a cross-sectional stock result into a time-series index result, which the source's own controls suggest is exactly the component that will not survive. If I am wrong it is in the optimistic direction: the true index-level effect is probably closer to zero than to my 0.2-point estimate, which would make the cost arithmetic even worse than stated.

name: Turn-of-the-month rebalancing window
source_claim: The turn-of-the-month effect - prices rising over roughly the last four and first three trading days of each month - is reported as the only calendar effect in S&P 500 FUTURES contracts that is 'statistically and economically significant and persistent over time.' Mean turn-of-the-month day return across indices is approximately 5 basis points. McConnell and Xu report that a strategy holding the S&P 500 during the turn-of-the-month and T-bills otherwise outperformed buy-and-hold by roughly 0.63% per year over 1928-1993. Recent work attributes the effect to infrequent rebalancing and risk deferral, amplified by overlapping rebalancing mandates, and finds the magnitude significantly larger after market turbulence and during recessions.

sources.title: Equity Returns at the Turn of the Month
sources.author_or_org: Wei Xu, John J. McConnell (Financial Analysts Journal)
sources.what_it_measured: Returns concentrated in the last and first few trading days of the month, 1926-2005, and a T-bill-switching strategy

sources.title: Infrequent rebalancing, risk deferral, and equity returns at the turn of the month
sources.author_or_org: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money
sources.what_it_measured: Rebalancing and risk-deferral mechanism behind the turn-of-the-month effect, and its conditioning on turbulence and recession

sources.title: Turn of the Month in Equity Indexes
sources.author_or_org: Quantpedia
sources.what_it_measured: Cross-index replication of the turn-of-the-month window; per-day magnitude around 5 bps

contradictory_evidence: This is the oldest and most widely published calendar anomaly in equities, which makes post-publication decay the default expectation rather than a risk. The Financial Planning Association's re-examination in the ETF era questions whether the return-enhancement strategies still work after implementation costs. The decisive practical problem is sample: over 2025-06 to 2026-09 there are only about 15 turn-of-month windows, so no test on our store can distinguish a 5 bps-per-day effect from zero regardless of whether it is real.
our_inference: OUR HYPOTHESIS is not that the lab should trade this, but that it belongs in the file as the reference point for what a genuinely low-turnover mechanism looks like against the cost constraint, and as a control variable. Any mechanism the lab does adopt should have its returns checked for whether they are concentrated in turn-of-month windows - if MR-01's overnight drift, for instance, turns out to be a turn-of-month effect in disguise, that is a materially different and much more fragile claim. This mechanism is worth one afternoon as a covariate and no more.
proposed_mechanism: Pension funds, target-date funds and balanced mandates rebalance on calendar boundaries, and salary and retirement contributions arrive at month end. Those flows are price-insensitive and clustered in a known window. The recent literature adds risk deferral: investors postpone re-entering risk until a structured rebalancing node, so demand accumulates and discharges at the boundary. It persists because the calendar is imposed by mandates and payroll cycles, not chosen by traders.
observable_variables: trading-day index within the month, counted from both ends
a turn-of-month flag for the last 4 and first 3 trading days
close-to-close return per session at 16:00 ET
session realised volatility, to test the 'larger after turbulence' conditioning
count of complete turn-of-month windows available in the store
failure_conditions: Pre-declared: this cannot be confirmed on our sample and should not be claimed as confirmed. It is killed as a standalone if the ~15 available windows do not produce a positive point estimate, and it is not accepted even if they do, because 15 observations cannot support the claim. Its only pass condition is as a covariate: if a mechanism the lab adopts loses significance once turn-of-month sessions are excluded, that mechanism is downgraded.
data_we_lack: Length of sample. This mechanism needs 20+ years to test and we have 1.25. Nothing else is missing - the trading-day calendar is derivable from the store itself.
falsification_test: Compute the mean 16:00-to-16:00 return on turn-of-month days versus all other days for ES and NQ, and report the count of windows alongside the t-statistic. The correct output of this test is almost certainly 'insufficient power,' and reporting it as such is the point.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points: 5 bps per day over 7 days is 35 bps, and 35 bps of ES at 7,600 is 26.6 points. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) for one round turn per monthly window, i.e. 1.2% and 1.9% of gross - by far the best cost ratio in the file. Per session the cost burden is 0.048 x 0.326 = 0.016 ES points. Cost is emphatically not the binding constraint here; statistical power is.
why_this_might_be_wrong: Fifteen observations. Even if the effect is exactly 5 bps per day and perfectly stable, the standard error on our estimate would be larger than the effect. Including it risks the lab spending time on something it cannot learn anything about from this data, and the most likely failure mode of this entry is that someone reads the excellent cost ratio and skips the power warning.

name: Pre-FOMC announcement drift
source_claim: Lucca and Moench (NY Fed Staff Report 512, Journal of Finance 2015): the S&P 500 rises on average 49 basis points in the 24 hours before a scheduled FOMC announcement, the returns do not revert in subsequent trading days, and over September 1994 to March 2011 this window accounted for roughly 80% of annual equity returns. No comparable effect appears in US Treasuries or money market futures, and similar pre-FOMC returns show up in other major international equity indices.

sources.title: The Pre-FOMC Announcement Drift (Staff Report 512)
sources.author_or_org: David O. Lucca, Emanuel Moench / Federal Reserve Bank of New York
sources.what_it_measured: Equity index and index futures returns in the 24 hours preceding scheduled FOMC announcements, 1994-2011

sources.title: The disappearing pre-FOMC announcement drift
sources.author_or_org: Finance Research Letters
sources.what_it_measured: Out-of-sample persistence of the pre-FOMC drift after the original publication

sources.title: The pre-FOMC announcement drift: short-lived or long-lasting? Evidence from financial and volatility markets
sources.author_or_org: Applied Economics
sources.what_it_measured: Whether the pre-FOMC drift persists in financial and volatility markets in more recent samples

contradictory_evidence: There is a paper titled 'The disappearing pre-FOMC announcement drift' (Finance Research Letters, 2021) finding the effect faded after publication - the same post-publication decay pattern the overnight drift shows. This is the second mechanism in this file whose originating institution has published its own obituary. On our sample there are roughly 10 FOMC meetings, which is not a sample.
our_inference: OUR HYPOTHESIS: the interesting version for this lab is not the pre-FOMC drift itself but the general class it belongs to - scheduled, calendar-known, price-insensitive-demand windows where a whole day's typical move is concentrated into a known hour. That class has by far the best cost arithmetic available to us, and the lab currently has no macro event calendar at all (data/events contains only earnings.json). Building an FOMC, CPI, NFP and quarterly-expiry calendar is a few hours of work and would unlock this whole class of low-turnover mechanisms, including the 08:30 ET and 14:00 ET release windows that Gao et al. identify as when intraday momentum is strongest.
proposed_mechanism: Lucca and Moench find no corresponding move in rates or money-market futures, which rules out the obvious explanation that the market is pricing the policy decision. The surviving explanations are a resolution-of-uncertainty risk premium paid to holders of equity risk into the announcement, or a systematic pre-positioning flow. Either way the timing is fixed by a published calendar, which is what makes it cheap to trade: one round turn per event, eight events a year.
observable_variables: FOMC announcement timestamps (NOT currently in the repo)
cumulative 1-minute return over the 24 hours ending at 14:00 ET on announcement day
realised volatility in the pre-announcement window versus its trailing average
the same construction for CPI (08:30 ET) and NFP (08:30 ET) release days
failure_conditions: Cannot be run at all until a macro calendar exists. Once it does: killed if the ~10 available FOMC windows produce a negative point estimate, and NOT accepted even if positive, because 10 events cannot support the claim. The correct use of this mechanism on our sample is as a contamination check - confirm that no other mechanism's edge is concentrated in FOMC windows.
data_we_lack: A scheduled macroeconomic event calendar. data/events/ contains only earnings.json. FOMC, CPI, NFP and quarterly expiry dates are all public and free; this is the single cheapest data addition in this file and it unlocks a class of mechanisms rather than one mechanism.
falsification_test: With an FOMC calendar in place, compute the mean cumulative return over the 24 hours ending at 14:00 ET on announcement days versus all other 24-hour windows, for ES and NQ, and report the event count next to the t-statistic. Expect 'insufficient power' and use the result as a contamination control for MR-01 through MR-07.
cost_feasibility_note: Magnitude is in ES points: 49 bps of ES at 7,600 is 37.2 points. Cost 0.326 ES points (ES) or 0.494 (MES) for one round turn per event, i.e. 0.9% and 1.3% of gross. Per session the cost burden is 0.032 x 0.326 = 0.010 ES points. Like MR-09, cost is irrelevant here and power is everything. The generalisable lesson for the lab is the ratio itself: a mechanism that concentrates a 37-point move into one known window costs 100x less to harvest than one that chases 1-point moves ten times a session.
why_this_might_be_wrong: Ten events, a documented post-publication disappearance, and a mechanism whose own authors could not explain it (no corresponding move in rates). The most likely truth is that the 49 bps was a 1994-2011 phenomenon that ended when it was published, and that the lab's return on this entry is the macro calendar it builds, not the trade.
